caseName: CityCenter Holdings, LLC v. Tutor Perini Building Corp. (Harmon Hotel Construction Defect Litigation)
citation: Case No. A-10-627691-B, Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County, Nevada
court: Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County, Nevada
keyFacts: Rebar installation defects discovered in 2008 during construction of the planned 47-story Harmon Hotel at MGM Resorts' $8.5B CityCenter development in Las Vegas rendered the structural steel-and-concrete tower unsafe to complete or occupy; MGM/CityCenter sued general contractor Tutor Perini (Perini Building Co.) for defective construction, and Perini countersued for unpaid contract balances. The dispute grew to roughly $500 million in claims and the unfinished tower was ultimately demolished (~$11.5M deconstruction cost) rather than repaired.
outcome: Global settlement reached on the eve of a trial expected to last over a year: MGM Resorts agreed to pay $153 million to Perini and $20 million to CityCenter/developer interests, which combined with roughly $85 million in prior insurance settlement proceeds brought CityCenter's total recovery on the Harmon defect claims to approximately $195 million.
dollarAmountBasis: Total settlement proceeds to CityCenter (prior ~$85M insurance settlement plus the December 2014 Perini settlement payments), as reported by ENR and MGM's SEC filing
notes: One of the largest and most litigated commercial construction-defect disputes in U.S. history (originally ~$500M in claims). Shows how a single structural discovery (misplaced/insufficient rebar) can escalate from a repair dispute into total loss of the asset (demolition) when the defect is deemed unsafe to remediate mid-construction. Cross-referenced against Las Vegas Review-Journal and ACS Lawyers coverage of the same settlement.

caseName: In re: Champlain Towers South Collapse Litigation
citation: Case No. 2021-015089-CA-01, Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida
court: Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida
keyFacts: The 12-story Champlain Towers South condominium in Surfside, FL partially collapsed on June 24, 2021, killing 98 people. Plaintiffs' central engineering theory (per court filings and NIST's ongoing investigation) was that original 1980s construction/design deficiencies in the building's pool-deck and foundation, worsened over decades and allegedly aggravated by vibratory sheet-pile driving for the adjacent Eighty Seven Park luxury condo's foundation construction, caused the collapse. Dozens of defendants were named including the condo association, the Eighty Seven Park developer (Terra Group/David Martin), its contractor, and its structural engineer.
outcome: Global class-action settlement of $997 million (potentially rising to ~$1.1 billion with sale of the site), funded primarily by insurance policies plus a reported $400 million specifically contributed by the developer, contractor, engineer, and subcontractors on the adjacent Eighty Seven Park project.
dollarAmountBasis: Total class-action settlement fund approved by the court, as reported by ENR, Commercial Observer, and wire coverage (later estimated to reach up to $1.1B with property-sale proceeds)
notes: Extreme outlier included for scale/context, not as a typical outcome. Distinct from more common construction-defect suits because it centers on wrongful-death/personal-injury damages, not just property/repair damages, and combines original-construction-defect theories with adjacent-construction-vibration causation theories against a separate development's contractor and engineer. Illustrates worst-case exposure for a structural/foundation defect claim implicating both an owner's original builders and a neighboring project's construction team.

caseName: Regalia on the Ocean Condominium Association, Inc. v. Regalia Beach Developers, LLC et al.
citation: Filed 2018, Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida (settled 2021, docket number not independently verified)
court: Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida
keyFacts: The condo association for the 46-story Regalia on the Ocean tower in Sunny Isles Beach (units priced $7.95M-$29.9M, home to Lionel Messi) sued developer Regalia Beach Developers LLC and Charleville Development Corporation, general contractor, and architect Arquitectonica, alleging improperly installed pool joints, unsafe steam rooms, and defective sliding glass doors across the building's 39 units.
outcome: Settled for $17.5 million, funded by insurers of the developer/contractor/architect defendants and some subcontractors: $9.6 million cash for repairs plus an $8.5 million markdown on replacement sliding glass doors for all 39 units.
dollarAmountBasis: Total disclosed settlement value ($9.6M cash + $8.5M in-kind door-replacement credit)
notes: Good illustration of a mixed cash-plus-in-kind settlement structure and of insurers (rather than the named defendants directly) funding the payout, which is common once CGL/E&O carriers step in to resolve defect claims.

caseName: Grandview at Riverwalk Port Imperial Condominium Association v. K. Hovnanian at Port Imperial Urban Renewal II, LLC et al.
citation: Hudson County Superior Court, New Jersey (Judge Jeffrey Jablonski), verdict June 1, 2017
court: Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Hudson County
keyFacts: The condo association for the six-story Grandview I building in West New York, NJ alleged the building was constructed with plywood subflooring appropriate only for a lower fire-safety classification (Type 2) when its layout actually required masonry/Type 3 construction, and that developer K. Hovnanian (a Hovnanian Enterprises subsidiary) knew of the code non-compliance but never obtained a valid reclassification. Architect RTKL New Jersey Architects was also sued for design negligence.
outcome: Jury awarded $3 million against the developer under the Consumer Fraud Act, automatically trebled to $9 million, plus attorneys' fees and costs; separately awarded $1 million against architect RTKL for professional negligence. The jury also pierced the corporate veil, holding parent Hovnanian Enterprises liable for the full judgment against its subsidiary.
dollarAmountBasis: Combined verdict: $9M against developer (trebled Consumer Fraud Act award) + $1M against architect RTKL, before separately awarded attorneys' fees/costs
notes: Notable for (1) corporate-veil piercing reaching the developer's parent company, (2) a Consumer Fraud Act treble-damages multiplier on top of the base construction-defect verdict, and (3) a materially smaller, separate design-negligence verdict specifically against the project architect -- useful benchmark for how architect exposure often runs well below developer/GC exposure in the same case.

caseName: Kellner v. Advance Cast Stone Co. (Milwaukee Parking Structure Panel Collapse)
citation: Milwaukee County Circuit Court, Wisconsin (incident June 2010; jury verdict reported 2013)
keyFacts: A 13-ton precast concrete facade panel fell from a Milwaukee parking garage, killing a 15-year-old bystander and injuring three others. Trial evidence showed subcontractor Advance Cast Stone had attached the panel with only two steel connecting rods instead of the four specified in the design, while general contractor J.H. Findorff and Son and owner Milwaukee County were also named as defendants and cross-claimed against each other over inspection and oversight responsibilities.
outcome: Jury awarded $39 million and apportioned fault: 88% to subcontractor Advance Cast Stone, 10% to general contractor J.H. Findorff and Son, and 2% to owner Milwaukee County -- an allocation that then governed each defendant's indemnification/contribution exposure.
dollarAmountBasis: Total jury verdict (wrongful death + personal injury damages), allocated 88%/10%/2% among subcontractor/GC/owner
notes: Strong benchmark for how comparative-fault allocation plays out in a multi-party construction-defect case: the specialty subcontractor that performed the defective connection work bore the large majority of liability (88%), the GC a modest share tied to oversight (10%), and the owner a small residual share (2%). Underlying defect (attachment devices) is a workmanship/negligence issue, but the case's core litigated question -- and its usefulness for the valuation tool -- is the fault-allocation/indemnification split among GC, sub, and owner.

caseName: Tropicana Casino Parking Garage Collapse Litigation
citation: Superior Court of New Jersey, Atlantic County (settlement approved April 2007)
court: Superior Court of New Jersey, Atlantic County
keyFacts: During October 2003 construction of a new parking garage at the Tropicana Casino Resort in Atlantic City, a section of the structure collapsed because concrete floors were not properly connected to the walls with required reinforcing steel/formwork -- OSHA cited contractor Fabi Construction for a willful violation for failing to erect and maintain formwork capable of supporting the loads. Four construction workers were killed and roughly 36 others injured. Plaintiffs sued Tropicana, parent Aztar Corp., and 15 other contractor/subcontractor defendants.
outcome: Settled for $101 million -- at the time reported as the largest construction-accident settlement in U.S. history -- structured as $82.5M cash, $8.2M workers' compensation payments, $8.3M for future medical expenses, and $2M in prior partial settlements.
dollarAmountBasis: Total approved settlement across all defendants, per NJ court approval reported by ABA Journal, Law.com/NJ Law Journal, and Insurance Journal
notes: Like Tropicana's, most of the largest disclosed construction-defect-adjacent settlements in this dataset involve a life-safety failure (collapse) during construction rather than a post-occupancy latent defect -- worth flagging for the valuation tool since these catastrophic-failure cases settle far above the range of typical envelope/waterproofing defect claims.

caseName: Confidential 88-Unit Condominium Development, Palm Springs, CA (ACTS Law arbitration/mediation)
citation: Arbitration/mediation, Riverside County, California (matter not independently docketed; law-firm-reported result)
court: Private arbitration/mediation (not a court of record)
keyFacts: Owners of an 88-unit Palm Springs condominium project retained ACTS Law in July 2021 over pervasive construction defects: vinyl windows and sliding glass doors warping/bowing and shattering in desert heat, dust/sand infiltration, water intrusion during rainfall, failed deck waterproofing, corroded steel overhang support posts, significant stucco cracking, and water trapped behind stone veneer.
outcome: After an initial failed mediation and an arbitration proceeding, the case resolved through a subsequent mediation in late 2024 for $9.75 million.
dollarAmountBasis: Total disclosed mediated settlement amount, per plaintiffs' counsel's press release
notes: Defendant names and precise property name were not disclosed in the source (law-firm client alert); property is described only as an 88-unit Palm Springs condo development. Useful as a real, recent (2024), disclosed-dollar example of a common defect pattern -- window/door product failure plus building-envelope water intrusion -- in a desert climate, resolved via mediation/arbitration rather than trial, which is the more typical path for mid-sized defect disputes than the large litigated cases elsewhere in this dataset.

caseName: Waiea Condominium Owners / Christopher Kim v. Nordic PCL Construction, Inc. and Howard Hughes Corp.
citation: First Circuit Court, State of Hawaii (Honolulu); Hughes Corp. v. Nordic federal suit filed late 2017, dismissed 2018; owner suits filed 2019
court: Circuit Court of the First Circuit, State of Hawaii
keyFacts: The 36-story, 177-unit Waiea luxury condo tower at Ward Village in Honolulu's Kaka'ako district (average unit sale price ~$3.6M) developed loud, recurring popping noises from its glass curtain-wall facade after opening in late 2016, along with water infiltration, faulty air conditioning, and inconsistent hot-water temperatures. Developer Howard Hughes Corp. first sued general contractor Nordic PCL Construction in late 2017 over the defects (and a separate ~$39M payment dispute); individual owners and the condo association filed their own suits in 2019 after the developer/contractor litigation stalled.
outcome: Howard Hughes Corp. committed to a repair/settlement package reported at $114.5-$116.5 million to remediate the facade and mechanical defects and resolve the condo owners' claims, with Hughes stating it would separately pursue recovery from GC Nordic PCL, which it blamed for the underlying construction flaws.
dollarAmountBasis: Developer's disclosed total commitment to fix defects/settle owner claims; some contemporaneous reporting cites $114.5M as the underlying repair-cost figure
notes: Reported figures vary slightly ($114.5M repair cost vs. $116.5M total settlement figure) across sources covering the same resolution; included at the higher, more commonly cited figure. Notable because the developer paid to fix/settle first and separately pursued indemnification against its general contractor -- a common sequencing where the party closest to unit owners (the developer/declarant) resolves consumer-facing claims before litigating cost recovery further down the contractual chain.

caseName: Park Hill Townhome Owners v. Hill/Gray Seven, L.L.C. et al.
citation: Circuit Court of the Ninth Judicial Circuit, Orange County, Florida, filed 2023
court: Circuit Court of the Ninth Judicial Circuit, Orange County, Florida
keyFacts: Owners of the 10-unit luxury Park Hill townhome community in Winter Park, FL (built for ~$15M, completed November 2019) sued developer Hill/Gray Seven, L.L.C. and 27 other contractor/subcontractor defendants alleging widespread manufactured-stone veneer attachment failures (including mechanical anchors drilled through the water-resistive barrier), defectively installed/incomplete waterproofing and windows causing water intrusion across all ten units, and undersized/misconfigured HVAC systems that caused humidity buildup requiring mold remediation.
outcome: Settled for $26.5 million across five consolidated related lawsuits (28 named defendants, 45+ law firms involved), announced August 10, 2026 -- approximately $2.65 million per unit.
dollarAmountBasis: Total disclosed settlement across the consolidated litigation, per plaintiffs' counsel's press release
notes: A useful recent (2026) high-per-unit-value benchmark: a small 10-unit luxury project generated a settlement exceeding many far-larger condo tower defect cases on a per-unit basis, illustrating how defect severity/pervasiveness (here, stone veneer, waterproofing, and HVAC failures across every unit) rather than building size drives claim value.

caseName: East Bridge Town Lofts Property Owners Association v. East Bridge Lofts, LLC, Creekstone Management, and Creekstone SC 1, LLC
citation: Charleston County Court of Common Pleas, South Carolina, jury verdict June 6, 2014
court: Court of Common Pleas, Charleston County, South Carolina
keyFacts: East Bridge Town Lofts, a 13-building, roughly 200-unit condominium community in Mount Pleasant, SC created by converting apartments to condos during the 2004-2006 real estate boom, developed serious construction problems after conversion. The owners' association sued developer entities East Bridge Lofts LLC, Creekstone Management, and Creekstone SC 1 LLC for negligence, breach of warranty, breach of fiduciary duty, unfair trade practices, and reckless negligence.
outcome: Jury verdict of $55 million: $22 million in actual damages plus $33 million in punitive damages -- described at the time as one of the largest residential/condominium real estate verdicts in South Carolina history.
dollarAmountBasis: Total jury verdict ($22M actual + $33M punitive damages)
notes: Notable for its large punitive-damages component (60% of the total award) tied to unfair-trade-practices and reckless-negligence findings against the developer specifically -- illustrates how apartment-to-condo conversion projects (also seen in the site's own 443 Greenwich St. case) can draw punitive exposure beyond ordinary negligence damages when a jury finds the developer's conduct especially culpable.

caseName: Mycon General Contractors, Inc. v. Employers Mutual Casualty Company et al.
citation: No. 3:26-cv-01098, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, filed April 6, 2026
court: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas
keyFacts: General contractor Mycon built the McKinney Corporate Center project in McKinney, TX (2013-2014). Beginning in 2016 the building's exterior masonry progressively deteriorated (foundation cracks, facade delamination), and by March 2024 large areas of facade had failed; the building's owner sued Mycon for defective stonework in March 2024. Mycon held continuous CGL coverage ($1M per-occurrence/$2M aggregate) from six insurers (Employers Mutual, Liberty, Amerisure, Hartford, Zurich, Arch) from December 2013 through 2025; Arch initially accepted the defense-cost claim before withdrawing coverage in April 2025, and all six ultimately denied coverage/duty to defend.
outcome: Pending as of filing. Mycon seeks more than $1 million in damages plus treble damages, exemplary damages, attorneys' fees, and 18% statutory interest for the insurers' denial of defense/coverage.
dollarAmountBasis: No disclosed settlement or judgment yet; complaint specifies only a damages floor of 'more than $1 million' plus statutory penalties
notes: Recent, actively pending case (filed April 2026) rather than a resolved one; included because it is a clean, real-world illustration of a facade/masonry progressive-deterioration claim triggering a multi-carrier CGL coverage fight, including one insurer (Arch) that began defending before withdrawing -- a fact pattern the valuation tool should be able to recognize even without a final dollar outcome yet.

caseName: Admiral Insurance Co. v. Tocci Building Corp.
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
keyFacts: General contractor Tocci Building Corp. and its insurer Admiral Insurance Co. disputed whether a CGL policy covered damage to non-defective parts of a Massachusetts construction project caused by a subcontractor's defective work on another part of the project. The district court found no duty to defend because the underlying suit did not allege 'property damage' caused by an 'occurrence'; the First Circuit affirmed on different grounds, holding the policy's 'Damage to Property' exclusion (j)(6) -- barring coverage for property that must be repaired/replaced because the insured's own work was performed incorrectly on it -- independently defeated coverage.
outcome: First Circuit affirmed that Admiral had no duty to defend Tocci in the underlying construction-defect suit.
dollarAmountBasis: Coverage-only appellate ruling; no settlement/judgment dollar figure for the underlying construction-defect claim disclosed in available reporting
notes: Published appellate opinion on legal doctrine (subcontractor-work exclusion) rather than a disclosed dollar outcome; included despite the project's preference for disclosed-dollar cases because it is a live, frequently-cited 2024 circuit split issue directly on point for the insurance_coverage_defect_dispute claim type, and materially affects whether a GC's own CGL policy will fund defense/indemnity for subcontractor-caused defects -- a threshold question that determines whether a contractor bears defect costs itself or shifts them to a carrier.

caseName: Cornice & Rose International, LLC v. Acuity
court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
keyFacts: Cornice & Rose, an architecture firm, oversaw construction of a building in Iowa; years after completion the building's owners and lender counterclaimed against Cornice for breach of contract and negligence over defects. Cornice held a CGL policy from Acuity and sought a defense; the district court initially found Cornice was not entitled to a defense.
outcome: The Seventh Circuit reversed, holding the architecture firm's insurer Acuity did owe a duty to defend under the CGL policy.
dollarAmountBasis: Coverage-only appellate ruling reversing denial of a defense; no settlement/judgment dollar figure for the underlying defect claim disclosed in available reporting
notes: A design professional (architecture firm), not a contractor, as the insured -- useful counterpoint to Admiral v. Tocci showing that duty-to-defend outcomes for CGL policies covering design professionals' construction-oversight role can come out favorably for the policyholder even in the same general 2024 wave of construction-defect coverage litigation.

caseName: Trustees of Princeton University v. Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects, LLP et al.
citation: No. 3:19-cv-21248, U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, filed December 2019
court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
keyFacts: Princeton University sued its architect, Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects (TWBTA), and structural sub-consultant Jacobs Engineering Group over design services for the 129,000-sq-ft Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment. The University alleged TWBTA and Jacobs failed to perform design responsibilities to the prevailing standard of care, causing unnecessary and excessive additional costs and roughly five months of project delay (the project finished about 10 months behind schedule, substantially completed January 2016).
outcome: Complaint sought $10.7 million for breach of contract including design negligence and delay-related costs; final resolution/settlement terms not disclosed in available reporting.
dollarAmountBasis: Amount sought in the complaint (breach of contract/design negligence, delay damages); outcome/settlement amount not publicly disclosed
notes: An institutional-owner-vs-architect design malpractice claim centered on delay/cost-overrun damages rather than physical building failure -- a useful counterpoint to the water-intrusion/structural fact patterns that dominate the rest of this dataset. Amount reflects the plaintiff's demand, not a confirmed final award; flagged accordingly.

caseName: Clark Construction Group, LLC v. Perkins Eastman DC, PC
citation: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, filed March 9, 2018; dismissed by joint stipulation 2020
court: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
keyFacts: Clark Construction, general contractor on the $2.5 billion mixed-use Wharf development in Washington, DC, sued project architect Perkins Eastman alleging the Phase 1 design documents contained substantial errors and omissions affecting structural columns, exterior retail doors, concrete beams, slabs, structural beams, terrace doors, stormwater cisterns, rebar, pier embeds, foundation piles, stairs, windows/curtainwalls, and acoustical isolation, plus professional negligence and negligent misrepresentation.
outcome: Clark and Perkins Eastman filed and then jointly dismissed their respective lawsuits in 2020, settling on confidential/undisclosed terms.
dollarAmountBasis: Amount sought in Clark's original complaint; final settlement terms were not disclosed by either party
notes: Direct GC-vs-architect design-error suit (rather than an owner-vs-design-team or owner-vs-GC-with-GC-then-suing-architect posture) on a large mixed-use commercial development; illustrative of how design errors surface as itemized, discipline-by-discipline defect lists (structural, envelope, MEP-adjacent) in GC pass-through claims, even though the final dollar recovery was kept confidential.

caseName: 300 Biscayne Boulevard Way Condominium Association v. Riverwalk East Developments LLC et al. (Aston Martin Residences)
citation: Filed April 15, 2026, Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida
court: Circuit Court of the 11th Judicial Circuit, Miami-Dade County, Florida
keyFacts: The condo association for the 66-story, 341-unit, ~$1 billion Aston Martin Residences tower in Miami sued developer Riverwalk East Developments, architect Revuelta Architecture International, GC Coastal Construction South Florida, structural engineer DeSimone Consulting Engineering, and roughly a dozen subcontractors less than two years after the tower's 2024 completion, alleging spalling concrete with exposed rebar, corroded steel around leaking pools/spas, cracked balcony slabs, seawall cracking, elevator defects, and leaking fire-suppression systems.
outcome: Pending as of filing; complaint seeks a minimum of $750,000 in damages plus compulsory repairs the association estimates will run into the millions once a full forensic assessment is complete.
dollarAmountBasis: Statutory/pleading minimum stated in the complaint; association's own estimate of true repair cost is materially higher but not yet quantified
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own already-tracked case list (js/data.js, id live-021 in the site data). Included as a very recent (2026), large-scale, multi-defendant example, though its disclosed dollar figure is only a pleading-stage minimum, not a settlement or final repair-cost figure -- the true exposure here is unresolved.

caseName: Board of Managers of the 443 Greenwich St. Condominium v. Metro Loft (Nathan Berman) and CetraRuddy Architecture
citation: Index No. 161174/2021, Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County (amended complaint March 11, 2024)
court: Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County
keyFacts: The condo board for 443 Greenwich Street, a 53-unit luxury conversion of a former Tribeca bookbindery, sued developer Nathan Berman's Metro Loft and architect CetraRuddy in December 2021 over pervasive structural and water-intrusion defects, including roof leaks that flooded multimillion-dollar penthouses and courtyard brickwork so deteriorated that decorative bricks could reportedly be pulled out by hand; an independent inspector characterized some violations as life-threatening.
outcome: An amended complaint filed March 11, 2024 raised the damages demand to $376 million; outside attorneys reviewing the filing estimated true exposure closer to $100 million once overlapping/duplicate claims are resolved. Litigation remains active (a September 2025 order granted summary judgment dismissing a related third-party claim); no final resolution of the core defect claims as of this writing.
dollarAmountBasis: Amended complaint's damages demand (pleading figure, not a settlement or judgment); independent estimate of likely actual exposure is closer to $100 million
notes: Sourced from CREdocket's own already-tracked case list (js/data.js, id live-018). Office-to-residential/factory-to-residential adaptive-reuse conversion defect case still in active litigation years after filing -- illustrates that pleaded demands in large defect cases can run 3-4x the outside estimate of true exposure, and that resolution timelines commonly stretch 4+ years from filing.
